description: Shin splints are not a toughness problem, they are an overwhelmed brake. Take the sixty-second toe raise test, learn how the tibialis catches your foot thousands of times a day, and get the graded plan that rebuilds the catcher instead of just resting it.

scenes.narration: Stand with your back against a wall, heels a step away from it, feet flat. Now lift the front of both feet toward your shins, heels glued to the floor, as high as they go, and lower them with control. That is one toe raise, and the burning muscle on the front of your shin is the one we are testing. Start a sixty second clock and count clean reps: full lift, full lower, no swaying off the wall, no bouncing at the bottom. When the lift shrinks to a twitch or the burn makes you stop, the test is over and the count is your number. Most runners who suffer shin splints are quietly shocked by how low this number is. Keep it. At the end, I will tell you what it says about your shins.

scenes.label: TOE RAISES IN SIXTY SECONDS
scenes.narration: Here is the line. Twenty five clean toe raises in a minute is where a shin stops being a complaint waiting to happen and starts being protected. Under fifteen, the muscle on the front of your shin is asleep at its job, and every run you take is being caught by tissue that was never trained to catch. Between fifteen and twenty five, the catcher is waking up and the margin is growing. Over thirty five, you own shin armor that most runners never build, because almost nobody trains the front of the leg. If your number is low, that is not bad news. It is the first explanation of your shin pain that comes with a training plan attached.
scenes.sub: under 15: shin is unprotected - over 35: runner's armor

scenes.narration: Look at the front of your shin, the muscle nobody poses with. That is the tibialis anterior, and its job is one of the most repeated in your whole life. Every time your heel strikes the ground, your foot wants to slap down flat, fast and uncontrolled. The tibialis is the brake that lowers it gently instead, catching your full momentum thousands of times a day. When that brake is strong, you never think about it. When it is overwhelmed, the pulling stress spreads along the shin bone where the muscle attaches, and the whole inner shin starts to ache. That ache is what the world calls shin splints. It is not the bone failing. It is a small, untrained brake being asked to catch a run it never prepared for, and brakes, unlike bones, can simply be trained stronger. Sit with that for a second, because it changes the whole problem. An overwhelmed brake is not a body breaking down. It is a training gap with a training solution, and the muscle involved is small, fast to respond, and asks for nothing but a wall and sixty seconds. Very few pain problems anywhere in the body come with a fix this cheap.

Now the pattern behind almost every case. Shin splints rarely arrive during easy weeks. They arrive right after a jump: the new running plan, the sudden daily walks, the sport season starting at full speed. Your enthusiasm can double your load in a week. The tissue along your shin cannot double its capacity in a week. It remodels on a slow clock, strengthening its attachments a few percent at a time, and it needs the load to grow in steps it can match. When load sprints and capacity walks, the gap between them is paid by the shin. This is also why complete rest feels like it works and then fails. Rest closes the gap by removing the load, but capacity never grew, so the first ambitious week reopens the exact same gap. The permanent fix is not less running forever. It is a stronger catcher and a staircase instead of a cliff.

Here is the detail that makes toe raises work instead of just burn. The tibialis does its real job while lengthening, lowering your foot against gravity after every step. So the training has to live in the lowering too. Lift the foot in one second, then lower it in three, slow enough that the front of the shin is working the entire way down. That slow lowering is called eccentric work, and it is the specific stimulus that teaches a brake to catch heavier loads. Rush the lowering and you are training the lift, which your shin barely uses. Slow it down and every rep becomes a rehearsal of the exact catch that running demands. Tempo is not a detail here. Tempo is the training.

Here is the skinny advantage, and this time it is physics. Every landing loads the shin brake with a multiple of your bodyweight. A lighter body pays a smaller bill on every single step, which means your tibialis can be trained daily, at high reps, without the sessions themselves becoming the overload that caused the problem. Heavy runners have to ration their shin work carefully. You can practice the catch every single day against a wall, in socks, in under two minutes, and recover by morning. The leg the mirror calls underdeveloped is, for this exact job, the efficient design: light feet with strong brakes beat heavy feet with tired ones on every run you will ever take.

Train with me. Back on the wall, heels down. Lift in one second, lower in three. Forty seconds of catches, twenty seconds of rest, three rounds. When the front of the shin burns, you are in the right building.

beats.text: REST UNTIL IT VANISHES, THEN SPRINT

scenes.narration: Here is your week. Toe raises every day, three rounds, always with the slow lowering. If you run, rebuild it as a staircase: walks first, then walk-jog intervals, then easy runs, adding a little each week and never two steps at once. Soft surfaces help while capacity grows. Now the mistakes. Resting until the pain vanishes and then returning at full mileage: retired, it is the exact loop that made the problem. Icing as the entire plan: retired, cold never built a brake. Pushing through sharp, worsening shin pain because runners are tough: retired. And the rule that matters most here: if the pain narrows to one pinpoint spot, hurts at rest, or aches at night, see a professional if it persists. Pinpoint bone pain is a different diagnosis, and it needs a scan, not a training plan.

So, your number. Under fifteen reps: your shin pain finally has a mechanical explanation, and it is the most fixable one on the list. Fifteen to twenty five: the catcher is training, keep the staircase slow and the count will climb. Over twenty five: your shins are protected, and your running can grow at the speed your tissue, not your ambition, sets. Put your count in the comments, just the number. In thirty days we stand at the same wall and count again. Shin splints do not heal by avoiding the catch. They heal when the catcher gets strong enough that the catch is easy.

Your shins were never fragile. Their brakes were just never trained. Train them a little every day, and in thirty days we count again together. Subscribe so the retest finds you. This is {channel}. Train the cable.

title: Stop Doing shin splints Wrong: Train Your tibialis healing Instead
